short_explanation: Low income can make it harder to afford enough nutritious food.
Unemployment can reduce household resources available for food.
High housing costs can compete with money available for food.
Food availability and affordability can shape dietary choices.
Food insecurity can push people toward cheaper, lower-quality foods.
Neighborhood conditions can affect opportunities to be physically active.
Diet patterns can influence energy balance and body weight.
Physical inactivity is an established risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.
Overweight and obesity are established risk factors for Type 2 diabetes.
Excess adiposity can contribute to insulin resistance.
Insulin resistance can impair normal glucose regulation.
Persistent elevated blood glucose is central to diabetes.
Increased thirst is a recognized symptom of diabetes.
Frequent urination is a recognized symptom of diabetes.
Fatigue is a recognized symptom of diabetes.
Blurred vision is a recognized symptom of diabetes.
Diabetes can damage nerves over time.
Diabetes can damage the kidneys over time.
Diabetes increases cardiovascular disease risk.
Diabetes increases stroke risk.
Diabetes can damage the eyes and threaten vision.
Diabetes can contribute to foot problems, partly through nerve and vascular damage.
Access to health care affects prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and ongoing management.
Food insecurity is associated with substantially higher prevalence/risk of Type 2 diabetes.
Physical inactivity may contribute to excess weight and metabolic risk.
Higher sodium intake can raise blood pressure and increase hypertension risk.
Physical inactivity is a recognized modifiable risk factor for high blood pressure.
Overweight and obesity increase the risk of developing high blood pressure.
Persistent stress can contribute to higher blood pressure directly and through related behaviors.
Access to screening, medication, follow-up, and team-based care affects hypertension detection and control.
High blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart and cardiovascular disease.
High blood pressure is a major modifiable risk factor for stroke.
High blood pressure can damage kidney blood vessels and contribute to chronic kidney disease.
Diabetes and high blood pressure commonly occur together, and diabetes increases hypertension risk.
Housing instability and unaffordable housing can increase the chance of living in substandard housing with leaks, mold, or other indoor hazards.
Air pollution and wildfire smoke can trigger asthma symptoms and attacks.
Mold exposure can trigger asthma symptoms or attacks in susceptible people.
Secondhand smoke is a recognized trigger for asthma attacks.
Dust mites, pests, pet allergens, and other indoor allergens can trigger asthma symptoms in susceptible people.
Emotional stress can trigger or worsen asthma symptoms in some people.
Access to clinicians, medicines, education, and follow-up affects asthma diagnosis and control.
Asthma can flare into an exacerbation or attack when airway inflammation and narrowing worsen.
Wheezing is a common symptom of asthma.
Shortness of breath is a common symptom of asthma.
Chest tightness is a common symptom of asthma.
Coughing, especially at night or early morning, is a common asthma symptom.
Obesity is associated with a higher risk of developing asthma and can worsen asthma symptoms.
Dietary patterns high in saturated and trans fats can contribute to high cholesterol.
Low physical activity can contribute to weight gain and an unfavorable cholesterol profile.
Obesity is linked with higher LDL and triglycerides and lower HDL cholesterol.
Type 2 diabetes can worsen cholesterol patterns and increase cardiovascular risk.
High cholesterol contributes to plaque buildup and coronary heart disease risk.
High cholesterol can contribute to atherosclerosis and stroke risk.
High blood pressure is a major risk factor for coronary heart disease.
Diabetes increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
Smoking is a major preventable risk factor for coronary heart disease.
Physical inactivity increases heart disease risk.
Obesity is associated with higher coronary heart disease risk.
Reduced coronary blood flow can cause angina or chest discomfort.
Coronary plaque can rupture or obstruct blood flow and cause a heart attack.
Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of COPD in the United States.
Secondhand smoke exposure is a recognized COPD risk factor.
Workplace dusts, fumes, and breathing hazards can increase COPD risk.
Poor outdoor air quality can worsen COPD symptoms and contribute to exacerbations in people with COPD.
A history of asthma is associated with higher COPD risk.
Chronic cough is a common COPD symptom.
Shortness of breath is a common COPD symptom.
COPD can flare into acute exacerbations with worsening respiratory symptoms.
Tobacco use is a causal risk factor for multiple cancer types.
Alcohol use increases the risk of several cancer types; risk generally rises with greater exposure.
Overweight and obesity increase the risk of multiple specific cancer types.
Higher physical activity is associated with lower risk of several cancer types; inactivity therefore marks higher risk for those cancers.
Cancer itself and cancer treatment can cause clinically important fatigue.
Long-term stress has been linked with depression risk, but it is one factor within a multifactorial disorder.
Lower social connection and social isolation are associated with greater depression risk.
Unemployment is consistently associated with increased depressive symptoms and major depression risk.
Housing insecurity and housing disadvantage are associated with worse mental health and depressive symptoms.
People with chronic diseases such as diabetes have a higher risk of depression; the relationship can operate in both directions.
Cancer and depression can co-occur, and some people with cancer have a higher risk of depression.
Sleep problems are common symptoms of depression.
Difficulty concentrating and making decisions are common depression symptoms.
Low energy and fatigue are common depression symptoms.
Access to mental health care affects screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up for depression.
